articles.title: Encrypted politics in the Global South: a decolonial systematic review of WhatsApp and political communication
articles.authors: Marcelo Santos, Tanja Bosch
articles.abstract: This article presents a systematic review of scholarly research on the political uses of WhatsApp, with a particular focus on studies conducted in or about the Global South. While research on digital politics has largely centered on open, platform-visible spaces such as Twitter and Facebook, WhatsApp constitutes a distinct political communication environment: encrypted, mobile-first, and shaped by vernacular practices that complicate visibility, data access, and governance. Drawing on a dataset of 239 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2016 and 2024 and indexed in Scopus, the review maps dominant themes, methodological approaches, geographic distributions, and patterns of authorship and collaboration in the field. The findings show that scholarship has overwhelmingly focused on misinformation, elections, and activism, often framing WhatsApp primarily through risk, harm, and regulation. In contrast, everyday political communication, participatory vernaculars, democratic affordances, and the mundane political uses of encrypted messaging remain comparatively underexplored. Methodologically, the literature is skewed toward surveys and content analysis, with limited use of ethnographic, critical, or computational approaches capable of engaging encrypted environments on their own terms. The review also reveals persistent structural asymmetries in knowledge production, including disparities in funding, institutional affiliation, collaboration patterns, language of publication, and epistemic authority, particularly between Global North institutions and Global South research contexts. Adopting a decolonial perspective, the article argues that the study of encrypted messaging platforms requires methodological and epistemological approaches attentive to opacity, infrastructural inequality, and locally grounded political practice. By theorizing the political affordances of encrypted communication and identifying key empirical and conceptual blind spots, the review contributes to debates in political communication and platform studies while positioning the Global South as a site of theoretical and methodological innovation rather than merely empirical application.

articles.title: Prompting with Respect: Cultural Norms and User Experience in LLM Interactions
articles.authors: Sujin Yang, Seoyoung Oh, Ha Eun Shim
articles.abstract: Despite growing interest in prompt engineering, its influence on user experience—particularly in relation to cultural communication norms—remains largely unexplored. This controlled experiment examined how respectful versus directive prompting—a culturally meaningful contrast in Korean—affects Korean users’ psychological experience during LLM interactions. Forty-three Korean female college students were randomly assigned to respectful prompt (RP) (using polite requests, compliments, and gratitude) or directive prompt (DP) (using imperatives, criticism, and performance-based penalties) conditions. Participants completed a writing task using ChatGPT. Results indicated that RPs yielded significantly higher satisfaction, particularly for affinity and likability, whereas the difference in perceived output quality was smaller and nonsignificant. Furthermore, RPs elicited socially supportive ChatGPT responses, whereas DPs were followed by apologies, suggesting bidirectional social adaptation between users and ChatGPT. Together, these findings suggest that culturally grounded communicative conventions may shape users’ subjective experience even where perceived output quality does not differ significantly, pointing to culturally adaptive large language model systems that recognize diverse communication patterns as essential design considerations rather than imposing universal paradigms.

articles.title: Balancing the scales of privacy: Perceptions of privacy issues and digital risk among domestic internet of things users
articles.authors: Cristina Paupini, Dominique Kost, Terje Gjøsæter
articles.abstract: While the proliferation of smart home technologies and the domestic Internet of Things (IoT) bring opportunities for a high level of control over household appliances and entertainment systems, it also presents challenges, not least in terms of privacy. In this study, we explore domestic IoT users’ perceptions of privacy issues and digital risk through in-depth semistructured interviews and digital home visits with 12 adults in 10 households in Norway. Based on the results of this study, we present a framework for an updated understanding of current privacy protection behaviors and decision-making from the perspective of domestic IoT users. Our “Scales of Privacy" model provides a holistic view of the process underlying the privacy calculus framework, incorporating both perceived risks and perceived benefits of data disclosure and including neutralizing factors, such as privacy cynicism and “nothing to hide” arguments. The results show a variety of perceived sources of risk, including national entities, technology companies, hackers, and partners/family. However, we highlight a discrepancy between the understanding of risk and perceived risk of our informants, on the one hand, and their actual behavior, on the other. We examine users’ stated reasons for utilizing an IoT-connected technology despite the risk, identifying five underlying motivations. Two were intrinsically related to the frictionless user experience provided by the devices (i.e., convenience and ease of use), whereas the remaining three (i.e., inevitability, unimpeachability and indiscernibility) revealed attitudes toward privacy protection partially influenced by a sense of being overwhelmed by the friction-filled experience of setting boundaries around personal data in the current digital environment.

articles.title: Safer sexting: Who cares and how?
articles.authors: Marina F. Thomas, Alice Binder, Jörg Matthes
articles.abstract: Sexting denotes technology-mediated sexual interactions from text messages to video calls. Involving sensitive data, safer sexting necessitates privacy management. Yet, digital privacy protection in intimate relationships remains understudied. We developed a four-factorial model of privacy strategies, the Sexting Privacy Management Inventory (SPMI). The SPMI distinguishes four kinds of privacy strategies along two dimensions: behaviors individuals employ alone or in interaction with their sexting partner (personal vs. interpersonal), and behaviors before or after sexting (preventive vs. reactive). As predictors of sexting privacy protection, we tested privacy concerns, romantic rejection sensitivity, sexting frequency, and sexting frequency in interaction with loneliness. Results of an online survey in a quota-based sample of 557 sexters (49.9% male) between 16 and 40 years (M = 28.97, SD = 6.67) confirmed the four-factor structure of the SPMI and showed differential effects for the four strategies. Privacy concerns against the sexting partner (social privacy concerns) predicted all privacy strategies, while concerns about how apps handle data (institutional privacy concerns) were unrelated to privacy protection. Individuals with higher romantic rejection sensitivity did not report less privacy management. More frequent sexting was related to more employment of privacy protection behaviors if individuals asynchronously sent storable files (e.g., pictures or videos). Effects of sexting frequency on privacy strategies were independent of loneliness. Thus, safer sexting was reported by those who were concerned about their sexting partner(s) and by frequent sexters (asynchronous). Overall, our four-dimensional model could be applied to other domains of privacy management.

articles.title: Disentangling the paradox of the privacy paradox on social media: The role of privacy dimensions, perceived benefits, privacy self-efficacy, and privacy cynicism
articles.authors: Laurent Wang, Tobias Dienlin, Miriam Metzger
articles.abstract: This study extends research on the ‘privacy paradox’ to the horizontal (privacy vis-à-vis peers) and vertical (privacy vis-à-vis institutions) dimensions of privacy on social media, and tests perceived benefits, privacy self-efficacy, and privacy cynicism as moderating factors for the privacy paradox on both dimensions. A cross-sectional online survey with a sample of U.S. adult social media users (N = 1,398) revealed no evidence for the privacy paradox on either the horizontal or the vertical privacy dimension (i.e., privacy concerns were positively associated with privacy management behaviors). Interestingly, perceived benefits and privacy cynicism moderated the relationships between privacy concerns and privacy management behaviors, though in the opposite direction to our prediction. In particular, the positive relationship between privacy concerns and privacy management behaviors was stronger among those with higher perceived benefits on the vertical dimension, and among those with higher privacy cynicism on both the horizontal and vertical dimensions. On the other hand, privacy self-efficacy was not a significant moderator on either dimension. Results demonstrate the multidimensional nature of online privacy and highlight the impact of conceptual and operational decisions on “finding” the privacy paradox.

articles.title: Adolescents’ social media use and conspiracy beliefs: The moderating role of rational and experiential thinking
articles.authors: Magdalena Iwanowska, Rosana Stan, Anna Maria Zawadzka
articles.abstract: A growing number of teenagers use social media, where they are frequently exposed to misinformation, including conspiracy theories. This cross-sectional study examines the relationships between social media use (with a focus on overall frequency and information-seeking use), tendency toward rational and experiential thinking, and conspiracy beliefs among adolescents from Romania and Poland. We hypothesized that while social media tends to spread conspiracy theories, such information is most likely to translate into beliefs among those with lower levels of rational thinking. The total sample comprised 561 participants (Mage = 17.27, SDage = 0.79). The results indicated that social media use for information-seeking—but not the frequency of social media use—positively predicts conspiracy beliefs among adolescents. However, tendencies toward both rational and experiential thinking moderated these relationships: the positive associations between social media use and conspiracy beliefs were significant only among adolescents with low or medium levels of rational thinking (for both frequency of use and information-seeking use), as well as among those with low or medium levels of experiential thinking (for information-seeking use only). We also found moderating effects for other purposes of social media use, specifically self-presentation and entertainment. In general, our study shows that the tendency toward rational thinking moderates the relationship between more purposes of social media use and conspiracy beliefs, suggesting that rational-analytical processing provides broader protection across different online activities.

articles.title: Comparative role of self-factors: A gender-based network analysis of problematic social media use and physical health
articles.authors: Jakub Helvich, Lukas Novak, Bibiana Jozefiakova, Eva Milkova, Peter Tavel
articles.abstract: The growing prevalence of problematic social media use (PSMU) and its negative association with health has become a significant public health concern. Despite increasing attention to its psychological correlates, there remains a critical need to investigate factors that might be associated with the co-occurrence of physical health and PSMU on a fine-grained level. This study aims to examine the symptom-level relationships between PSMU, physical health, self-esteem, and self-compassion and investigate potential gender differences in these relationships. A sample of 2912 Czech adults (Age: M = 27.6, SD = 12.3, Females: 61.02%) was used to examine the relationships. A stratified network analysis based on undirected mixed graphical models and network comparison tests were conducted to inspect the gender differences. Distinct gender-specific patterns were found. In women, the use of social media to escape negative emotions emerged as a bridge symptom linking PSMU with physical health. In men, fewer and weaker connections were observed between specific PSMU and physical health symptoms. Self-esteem bridged a new cluster of physical health symptoms through escape-use in both genders. Self-compassion bridged escape-use with physical health symptoms in women, whereas no direct associations were observed in men. However, the inclusion of self-compassion in the men’s network was associated with changes in existing connections, making all links between PSMU and physical health absent. These findings highlight the gender-specific nature of PSMU and underscore the need for nuanced approaches when fostering potentially protective factors that may be relevant to physical health.

articles.title: Immerse & befriend: The role of synthetic relationship perception and narrative transportation in a mental health app
articles.authors: Marisa Tschopp, Stefanie H. Klein, Christine Anderl, Henrik Sætra, Sonja Utz
articles.abstract: The global mental health crisis has driven the rise of apps using conversational agents (CAs) to complement or replace human professional support. Offline, the success of such interventions often depends on the relationship between the help-seeker and the support provider. Online, psychological processes elicited by specific app features relating to the CA and its unique story design might play a significant role. However, research on these processes and their consequences on user engagement and well-being is scarce. To shed light on this, we conducted a cross-sectional study with 348 active users of the mental health app Betwixt. The app integrates a scripted CA as a mentor, guiding users through levels of self-development within a dream-like fantasy narrative. We tested how perceived synthetic relationships with the CA (based on the Relational Models Theory, Fiske, 1992) and narrative transportation (i.e., the extent to which users become absorbed in the story) relate to app engagement and perceived stress. Our findings indicate that a strong sense of narrative transportation and perceiving the CA as friend-like positively predict hedonic benefits and future usage intentions. However, these factors were not significantly associated with perceived stress. Our results contribute to the emerging field of synthetic relationships and highlight the potential of narrative transportation for developers of apps using similar designs. We also discuss the ethical concerns of fostering friend-like relationships with CAs and their practical implications for developers and mental health professionals.

articles.title: Online connectedness: The meaning of online social interactions for young adults with mild intellectual disabilities
articles.authors: Johanna Lucia Louise Van Alem, Noud Frielink, Wieneke Penninga, P.J.C.M. Embregts
articles.abstract: Young adults with mild intellectual disabilities are increasingly engaging in online social interactions. While online participation offers these young adults opportunities for connection, research on their perspectives remains scarce. Therefore, this study explores their experiences and interpretations of online social interactions. Six Dutch young adults aged 19–31 years old with mild intellectual disabilities participated in semi-structured interviews, which were analysed using interpretative phenomenological analysis. Four experiential themes were identified: 1) online connections feel important, yet offline connectedness remains essential, 2) balancing between the wish and reality of fitting in online, 3) online safety as an ongoing learning process, and 4) feeling and dealing with the dark sides of online interactions. The current study concludes that online interactions can enrich, but do not replace, offline social relationships. Nevertheless, positive online interactions are not self-evident; our findings underscore the importance of strong and supportive offline networks for fostering safer, more meaningful online contact and enhancing resilience to negative experiences.

articles.title: Bridging the digital divide: How smartphones are associated with physical, psychological, and social well-being in marginalized groups
articles.authors: Ilenia Gasparini, Marco Marinucci, Luca Pancani, Paolo Riva
articles.abstract: This paper examines the digital divide by investigating how smartphone use and digital exclusion are associated with the physical, psychological, and social well-being of marginalized populations—including migrants, people experiencing homelessness, and prisoners—across five correlational studies (total N = 817). The findings reveal both benefits (e.g., fostering integration and connection) and drawbacks (e.g., exacerbating psychological challenges) of smartphone use. Study 1 explored smartphone usage among migrants (N = 278), showing that information-seeking apps (e.g., location services) were positively associated with psychological need satisfaction, physical health, and adaptation, whereas communication apps were not significantly associated with any of the outcome variables. Studies 2a (N = 75) and 2b (N = 174) focused on migrants during their migration journeys. In Study 2a, smartphone use for communication was positively associated with adaptation. In contrast, using smartphones for emotional regulation was linked to poorer psychological well-being in both studies. Study 3 investigated smartphone use among people experiencing homelessness (N = 71), revealing that communication was positively associated with psychological health, whereas use for emotional regulation was tied to lower psychological well-being. Finally, Study 4 examined prisoners (N = 219), linking limited technological skills to poorer physical and psychological well-being, while lack of access alone was not significantly associated with these outcomes. Overall, the results point to meaningful links between smartphone use and experiences of integration and connection among marginalized groups, as well as to poorer psychological well-being associated with using smartphones for emotion regulation and to the adverse effects of digital exclusion.

articles.title: Associations between prior parental mediation and digital wellbeing among young adults: Incorporating both variable- and person-centered approaches
articles.authors: Wei Ren, Suchuan Ma, Kaili Wang
articles.abstract: Amid pervasive digital connectivity, maintaining digital wellbeing is increasingly important for young people. Yet empirical research on the relationship between parental mediation and digital wellbeing remains limited. Incorporating both variable- and person-centered approaches, this study explores the associations between prior parental mediation, digital disconnection and digital wellbeing among young adults. Data were drawn from 994 Chinese first-year college students (aged between 15 to 22), a developmental stage marked by increasing autonomy over digital life. Variable-centered analyses indicated that only prior active mediation was significantly associated with digital wellbeing, with rule-based disconnection mediating this association. Latent profile analysis showed that most parents practiced different mediation strategies in a balanced way. Five distinct youth-perceived mediation patterns were identified: moderate-involved (37.12%), low-involved (31.79%), high-involved (16.00%), supportive (10.97%), and restriction-oriented (4.12%). articles.title: Perceptions of AI-generated profile pictures: Effects on quality, attractiveness, and trustworthiness
articles.authors: Jacob Long, Jingyi Xiao, Shamira McCray, Ertan Ağaoğlu, Abdullah Alajmi, Chinwendu Akalonu, Yanzhen Xu
articles.abstract: This study investigates perceptions of AI-generated profile pictures and how disclosure of AI use shapes impressions. In a preregistered experiment, U.S. adults (N = 817; ages 18–99, M = 47.83, SD = 18.79; 48% men and 50% women) evaluated what they were told were social media profile pictures. The 2 × 2 factorial design varied whether images, all with a professional headshot style, were AI-generated and whether they were disclosed as AI-generated. Across three outcomes, AI-generated images were rated as higher quality than professional photos of the same subjects, but disclosure that an image was AI-generated reduced perceived quality. On average, AI generation and disclosure did not significantly affect perceptions of the person's social attractiveness or trustworthiness. Exploratory analyses indicated that self-assessed AI knowledge moderated responses to disclosure: lower-knowledge respondents downgraded labeled images and the depicted person, whereas higher-knowledge respondents evaluated labeled images and the person more positively. Taken together, the findings suggest that disclosure of AI use primarily affects evaluations of the image as an object rather than person-level impressions.

articles.title: Should I speak or should I go? Relationship closeness and descriptive norms on reactions to hate memes in private chat groups
articles.authors: Christina Josupeit
articles.abstract: Visually and humorously packaged hate messages spread quickly on social media and thus may be shared in private chat groups, where they may trigger conflicts. In such situations, individuals must decide whether to speak up, remain passive, and/or leave the group. This study investigates how relational dynamics influence individual responses in such potentially contentious situations. Specifically, we examined the effects of relationship closeness and conformity to descriptive norms on the intention to comment and the intention to leave a group following the posting of a racist meme. A total of 1,090 German-speaking participants (60% female, 40% male, 1% diverse) with a mean age of 49.8 (SD = 13.84, range = 24–87) took part in an online experiment. Participants were randomly assigned to one of six conditions in a 2×3 factorial design, manipulating relationship closeness (low, high) and group response to a racist meme (no reaction, full reaction, mixed reaction). Higher relationship closeness to the group significantly increased the intention to comment on the meme, whereas participants in the high-closeness condition reported a significantly lower intention to leave the group. Contrary to expectations, group response had no significant effect on the intention to comment, challenging assumptions about conformity pressures in online groups. The results suggest that relationship closeness is more influential than mere descriptive norms in private group settings, contributing to a refined understanding of social impact and conformity processes in digital environments.

articles.title: Media-multitasking and attentional control: A theory-driven research agenda
articles.authors: Elger Abrahamse, Douglas Parry, Daniel Le Roux, Susanne Baumgartner
articles.abstract: Mobile digital technologies provide ample incentives and opportunities for media-multitasking, and media consumption has become almost synonymous with media-multitasking as a result. Concerns have been raised about the potential sustained impact of media-multitasking on attentional control, and ample empirical studies have been devoted to this topic. However, recent reviews and meta-analyses demonstrate that cross-sectional outcomes on the relationship between media-multitasking and attentional control remain inconsistent and inconclusive. This obstructs theoretical advancement regarding sustained impact and, consequently, hinders clear insight into the question about whether, when, and for whom remedial interventions should be considered. In the current paper, we argue that extant research has suffered from a collective failure to consider relevant intra-individual variation in attentional control. We investigate the theoretical and methodological implications of this neglect for the study of sustained media-multitasking effects on attentional control, outlining the tenets of a theory-driven research agenda to guide a new generation of cross-sectional studies. These will be much needed in providing the evidence base to justify and inform more resource-intensive causal research in this field.

articles.title: When fast becomes too fast: Working memory constraints in accelerated video playback
articles.authors: Hyenyeong Chung, Yunju Nam, Upyong Hong
articles.abstract: This study investigated whether accelerated video playback affects cognitive load and comprehension, focusing on the moderating role of working memory capacity. With speed control widely available on digital platforms, it is crucial to understand how individuals cognitively process video content presented at varying speeds. To examine this, eye movements were recorded while 38 participants (16 males, 22 females; age range = 19–26 years, M = 22.5, SD = 1.9) watched information-oriented videos at varying speeds, followed immediately by a recall test. Results indicated that as playback speed increased, perceptual load increased for all participants. However, cognitive load and comprehension patterns differed by working memory capacity. Individuals with lower working memory capacity showed shallow processing, as indicated by the absence of elevated cognitive load, and exhibited significantly reduced accuracy in recall tasks. This suggests that they were unable to sufficiently process and retain key information due to the limitations in their cognitive resources. In contrast, individuals with higher capacity showed increased cognitive load under high-speed conditions yet maintained stable recall performance. This implies that their greater capacity to process information enabled deep processing and successful transfer to long-term memory. These findings highlight the importance of considering individual cognitive differences when evaluating the effectiveness of speed-watching strategies. Working memory capacity critically determines how well viewers can cope with the rapid presentation of multimodal content. Ultimately, our findings suggest that speed adjustment may not be an efficient strategy for all users, highlighting the need for cognitively responsive designs that foster user-centered ICT environments.

articles.title: AI-based writing assistants for emotional tone: Investigating users’ acceptance and recipients’ perceptions in online negotiations
articles.authors: Josephine Hagedorn, Roman Klinger, Kai Sassenberg
articles.abstract: With the use of AI, modern writing-assistants can offer users recommendations on more subjective, socially relevant communication style aspects like emotional tone. While these recommendations commonly aim to affect interpersonal interaction outcomes, user acceptance determines the recommendations’ actual impact on the resulting messages and potential downstream effects on message recipients. The present research aimed to investigate this interplay of an AI-based writing-assistant’s recommendations for emotional tone, users’ acceptance, and recipients’ perceptions of the messages and the sender. Two online experiments used the context of online negotiations (Ntotal = 1,532, native English speakers residing in the UK) to investigate if users’ acceptance of a writing assistant for emotional tone was affected by whether its recommendations a) utilized AI-based functionalities and b) promoted a positive or negative emotional tone. Users tended to show greater acceptance of AI-based than non-AI recommendations, independent of whether a positive or negative emotional tone was recommended. A third study (N = 408) then investigated recipients’ perceptions of the produced messages. Recipients’ ratings of revised and original messages differed significantly regarding the messages’ emotional tone, their interpersonal impression of the messages’ sender, and their willingness to make concessions. Results thus suggest that the examined recommendations can elicit revisions to the emotional tone of interpersonal messages in the recommended direction and that these changes consequently affect the messages’ social effects. Hence, the present research illustrates the relevance of AI-based functionalities in writing-assistants for users’ acceptance and potential effects on interpersonal interaction outcomes once messages are sent.

articles.title: No evidence of protection: Imaginary bulletproof glass fails to reduce psychological harm in content moderation
articles.authors: Chloe McDonough, Sarah Lewitzka, Victoria Bridgland, Ella Moeck, Reginald Nixon, Carolyn Semmler, Melanie Takarangi
articles.abstract: Content moderators exposed to graphic content online are at risk of negative mental health outcomes including depression, anxiety and distressing intrusive thoughts—a hallmark symptom of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Yet, there is little research on strategies to protect people exposed to graphic content. Here, we empirically tested a strategy suggested on a range of online sources for handling traumatic imagery–visualizing bulletproof glass exists between oneself and the screen. Using a content moderator simulation paradigm with Amazon Mechanical Turk participants (N = 202), we experimentally tested whether this intervention reduces outcomes associated with exposure to graphic imagery. We found no empirical support for this intervention influencing intrusive thought frequency, negative intrusion characteristics like intensity, anxiety, positive affect, or negative affect. We conclude that this bulletproof glass strategy should not be recommended to groups exposed to graphic content, like content moderators.

articles.title: Improving fintech services through human–machine interactions: user anthropomorphic perception through an affordance lens
articles.authors: Atta Addo, Dana Lunberry
articles.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how technology features influence anthropomorphic perceptions among users, focusing on interactive technology such as interactive voice response (IVR). By employing a sociotechnical framework, the study emphasises the role of design affordances in fostering human-like qualities in digital systems, particularly within financial services contexts. Design/methodology/approach Using a case study methodology, the research examines IVR technology deployed to financial savings clients at a Ghanaian savings and loans institution. Data were collected through user interactions and analysed through an affordance lens to identify key design elements that evoke anthropomorphic perceptions. Findings The study identifies ways in which the IVR system evoked human-like qualities. These were shaped by design affordances, including personalised voice messages, culturally relevant content and a consistent human-like persona. The findings reveal how user emotions and imagination mediate anthropomorphic perceptions in digital system interactions. Research limitations/implications The study is limited to a single case in a specific cultural and financial context, which may affect generalisability. Future research should explore diverse contexts and technologies to validate the findings and expand understanding of anthropomorphic design. Practical implications Insights from this study inform the design of culturally attuned and user-friendly digital systems. By leveraging anthropomorphic features, financial services can foster greater trust, engagement and user satisfaction in their technology solutions. Social implications Anthropomorphic design can improve access to financial services, especially for underbanked populations, by enhancing usability and trust in digital platforms. This approach also supports inclusive technology design that respects cultural nuances. Originality/value This study offers a novel sociotechnical perspective on anthropomorphism in Information Systems research, demonstrating how design affordances evoke human-like perceptions. It provides actionable guidance for designing engaging and culturally relevant digital systems in financial services.

articles.title: Reducing supply chain uncertainty via blockchain: an affordance and transaction cost perspective
articles.authors: Wilson K.S. Leung, Man Kit Chang, Man Lai Cheung, Si Shi, Randy Yee Man Wong
articles.abstract: Purpose This study examines how blockchain technology supports uncertainty reduction and collaboration in supply chains, thereby improving perceived business process performance. Drawing on affordance theory and transaction cost theory, we investigate how transparency and traceability affordances reduce environmental and partner-related uncertainties and facilitate supply chain collaboration. Design/methodology/approach We collected data from 297 supply chain managers in China. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to test the proposed relationships among blockchain affordances, uncertainty reduction, collaboration and performance outcomes. Findings The results show that the traceability affordance significantly reduces all types of uncertainty, while the transparency affordance indirectly contributes to uncertainty reduction through traceability. Reduced uncertainty strengthens supply chain collaboration, which in turn improves perceived business process performance. Research limitations/implications This study identifies uncertainty reduction as a key mechanism linking blockchain affordances to supply chain collaboration and perceived business process performance. As the study focuses primarily on uncertainty within transaction cost theory, future research could examine other transaction characteristics and contextual conditions that shape blockchain affordances and their consequences. Practical implications Managers should establish supply chain transparency while prioritizing traceability for high-risk products and suppliers. Blockchain-enabled audit trails can support supplier evaluation, transaction verification and contract monitoring, providing a stronger informational basis for interorganizational collaboration. Originality/value This study explains how blockchain affordances translate into collaborative and performance outcomes through uncertainty reduction. The findings further distinguish the roles of transparency and traceability in this process, providing a more nuanced understanding of how blockchain creates value in supply chain relationships.

articles.title: Loneliness and the local news environment
articles.authors: Danny Hayes, Anusha Trivedi
articles.abstract: Recent research suggests that changes to the media environment have contributed to loneliness in the United States. This work focuses on smartphones and social media, with the decline of local news receiving little attention. We argue that local news promotes social well-being by informing residents about their communities, fostering attachment and a sense of belonging that can reduce loneliness. We provide evidence in two studies. First, using state-level data and multiple measures of news availability, we show that loneliness is higher in states with fewer options for local news. Second, we find in a nationally representative survey that people who rarely consume local journalism report greater loneliness than regular local news consumers. There is some evidence that the relationship is strongest in rural areas, which have experienced severe declines in local news access. We conclude by proposing a research agenda to further explore how community news may support social well-being.

articles.title: Looking good, fitting in: co-trajectories of appearance- and friendship-related identity distress and positive online self-presentation in adolescence
articles.authors: Gaëlle Vanhoffelen, Lara Schreurs, Laura Vandenbosch
articles.abstract: Adolescence is a critical period for identity development, often accompanied by identity distress. Simultaneously, adolescents are also preoccupied with presenting themselves as positive as possible on social media, which may reflect and reinforce identity distress. Yet, the dynamic associations between adolescents’ identity distress and positive online self-presentations remain unexplored. Accordingly, this three-wave panel study among adolescents from Belgium, France, and Slovenia (N = 1,697; Mage = 15.14, SDage = 1.78, 57.2% girls) used Latent Class Growth Analysis to identify distinct co-trajectories of identity distress and positive online self-presentation in the domains of friendship and appearance over one year. The findings showed that identity distress and positive self-presentations can follow maladaptive, (high risk) adaptive, or stable co-trajectories over time, depending on the identity domain, adolescents’ demographic, and social media use characteristics. In doing so, the study provides novel evidence on the heterogeneous co-development of adolescents’ identity distress and online self-presentation.

articles.title: Quality Over Quantity? Couple Financial Communication and Relationship Satisfaction
articles.authors: Johanna Peetz, Matthew T. Saxey
articles.abstract: The present study examined the reciprocal associations between both couple members’ reports of financial communication and relationship satisfaction over the course of a month ( N = 136 couples). Both partners reported more subjectively frequent and higher-quality financial discussions when their initial relationship satisfaction was higher, though these links appeared particularly strong for women. The quality of financial communication during the month was, in turn, associated with their own and their partner’s relationship satisfaction at the end of the month, even after accounting for baseline satisfaction. In contrast, greater frequency of financial communication did not show similar benefits for the relationship. Household income and income disparity between partners did not moderate the links between satisfaction and financial communication. However, the link between communication quality and satisfaction was moderated by financial integration (stronger among couples who fully pool their finances), and the link between communication frequency and satisfaction was moderated by subjective financial stress (positive link among those who felt stressed, negative link among those who did not feel stressed). Overall, these findings suggest short-term, reciprocal associations between financial communication quality and relationship satisfaction, whereas communication frequency appeared to somewhat reflect initial relationship satisfaction rather than also predict later satisfaction.

articles.title: Adult Children’s Chronic Health Conditions and Intergenerational Financial Transfers Between Parents and Early Midlife Adult Children: Variation Across Sons and Daughters
articles.authors: Anna Hammersmith, Xing Zhang
articles.abstract: As our population ages, adult children and parents will experience greater overlap across their lives, offering more opportunities to engage in intergenerational financial transfers. Intergenerational transfers benefit both generations. They may be especially crucial as parents encounter challenges associated with aging, and as adult children grapple with their own health problems. We used the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health data to explore whether an adult child’s chronic health conditions in young adulthood were associated with financial transfers between early midlife adult children and their parents, factoring in differences between sons and daughters. More specifically, we examined the dynamics of upward, downward, and mutual financial transfers among adult children reporting no chronic conditions, one chronic condition, two chronic conditions (multimorbidity), or three or more chronic conditions (severe multimorbidity). Our results indicate adult children with severe multimorbidity were more likely than adult children without chronic health conditions to receive downward financial transfers from their parents. Moreover, adult children with multimorbidity were more likely than adult children without chronic health conditions to engage in mutual financial transfers. Regarding gender of the adult child, we found among children reporting one chronic condition, sons were less likely to engage in downward, upward, and mutual transfers with parents relative to daughters. This research advances our understanding of how an adult child’s chronic health conditions shape dynamics of financial transfers with parents.

articles.title: Keeping and Deleting Messages in Ongoing Romantic Relationships: Extending the Virtual Relationship Memory Model
articles.authors: Md Ibnun Sarwar Rafi, Jessica R. Frampton
articles.abstract: People frequently decide which virtual objects (e.g., messages, photos) exchanged with romantic partners to keep or delete. The virtual relationship memory model (VRMM) argues these decisions help shape relational memories and meaning. However, the model was developed in the context of relationship dissolution. The present study extends the VRMM to the context of ongoing romantic relationships. Specifically, this study consisted of 30 semi-structured interviews with adults who reported on their motivations for keeping or deleting virtual objects, the perceived consequences of such decisions, and the ways in which network members influence their decision processes. Findings showed that participants kept virtual objects as relational memory resources and for partner accountability, whereas deletion served emotion regulation, conflict management, impression management, and privacy functions. Deletion created uncertainty within the relationship depending on message content and relational context, and network members influenced message management choices. By extending the VRMM to ongoing relationships, this study reframes virtual relational memory not only as a retrospective account of past relationships, but also as an ongoing communicative process. Additionally, it identifies motivations and consequences of message management unique to intact relationships.

articles.title: Disappearing Voices, Emerging Resistance: Journalism, Language, and Social Inequality in the U.S.-Mexico Borderlands
articles.authors: Jessica Retis, Susan Barnett, Liliana Lopez Ruelas
articles.abstract: This article examines how linguistic, geographic, and racial inequalities shape journalism in the U.S.-Mexico borderlands. Focusing on Southern Arizona, it analyzes the rise of two community-driven Spanish-language news startups following the closure of the city’s only Spanish-language newspaper. Emerging in connection with a bilingual journalism initiative at a local university, these projects developed through collaborative research, community engagement, and newsroom experimentation aimed at addressing gaps in local news coverage. Drawing on research-action practices, collaborative research, and self-ethnography, the study examines how marginalized communities resist exclusion by producing culturally relevant media. It situates these efforts within broader discussions of news deserts, institutional inequality, and the systemic neglect of linguistic minorities, offering insight into how grassroots journalism—and the institutional spaces that can help incubate it—can challenge dominant media norms and reimagine local news in underserved, multilingual communities.

articles.title: More Clickbait, But Fewer Shares? Unpacking the Relationship Between Multimodal Sensationalism and Online User Engagement
articles.authors: Xucheng Cao, Shuhua Zhou, Jinye Zhu, Xiaohui Wang
articles.abstract: This study examined multimodal sensationalism by analyzing how textual and visual sensationalist features embedded in video headlines and thumbnails relate to user engagement. Using a hybrid human-large language model content analysis, we identified 15 sensationalist features across 1,100 trending videos from Douyin. The results show that legacy news outlets used fewer textual sensationalist elements, particularly Internet slang, hashtags, and positive emotions, than non-journalistic producers. Additionally, visual sensationalist features exhibited an inverted U-shaped relationship with user engagement. These findings advance understanding of the nonlinear and modality-specific effects of sensationalism and offer practical insights into the optimal use of multimodal sensationalism on social media.

articles.title: Diffusion, Logics, and Boundaries: How Journalists in Marginalized Media Markets Negotiate AI in Newsrooms
articles.authors: Dren Gërguri, Jennifer Sorrells, Gheorghe Anghel, Maximiliano Frías, Antonia Matei, Ramadan Çipuri, Stela Lechpammer, Emel Arık, Irena Lovrenčič Držanič
articles.abstract: Literature on artificial intelligence (AI) and its role in journalism is expanding rapidly. Yet it remains disproportionately focused on Western contexts, ignoring how AI is perceived and negotiated in marginalized or semi-peripheral markets. This article focuses on how journalists in Albania, Croatia, Kosovo, North Macedonia, Romania, Slovenia, and Turkey perceive, apply, and challenge AI technologies. Drawing on theories of diffusion of innovations, institutional logics, and boundary work, this study analyzes the presentation of AI as both a technological innovation and a symbolic threat to professional identity. We conducted 10 focus-group sessions with 68 journalists and editors from diverse media outlets in seven different countries. Sessions were audio-recorded, transcribed, and thematically analyzed. Transcripts were independently coded by two researchers using AI-assisted coding in ATLAS.ti, alongside standard manual coding, with consensus-building to refine the process. The results show skewed and uneven AI implementation, motivated by efficiency requirements and not institutional strategy. Journalists present AI as a helping hand, noting concerns about fact-checking, editorial control, and professional autonomy. These strains indicate conflicting institutional logics, especially between technological efficiency and professional norms, and produce particular kinds of boundary work. Whereas defensive strategies underline the unreliability of human judgment, adaptive strategies also incorporate AI under editorial oversight. The article is relevant to the literature because it emphasizes ways in which structural limitations, institutional stresses, and professional ideals influence AI adoption outside of Western media systems.

articles.title: Giving AI a Body: Representations of Social Robots in Latin American Media
articles.authors: Iliana Ferrer, Leonor Balbuena, Oscar Mario Miranda-Villanueva, Mathias-Felipe De-Lima-Santos
articles.abstract: Social robots (physically embodied systems designed to interact with humans through social behaviours) have gained increasing visibility in news media. However, their everyday presence in Latin America remains limited, reflecting broader asymmetries in technological diffusion across non-WEIRD contexts. This study examines how social robots are represented in Latin American news media and how artificial intelligence (AI) is communicated through embodied technologies. A quantitative content analysis was conducted on a corpus of 404 news articles published in Spanish and Portuguese language media, retrieved through Google’s search engine. The study employs an LLM-assisted coding procedure combining automated classification with human validation. The analysis focuses on three dimensions: journalistic treatment (narrative frames and evaluative tone), representation of AI (attributed agency and explicit references to AI), and social functions (social roles, sectors of application, and sources). The findings show that coverage is predominantly framed around care and assistance, with positive or ambivalent evaluations, while conflict-oriented frames remain marginal. Social robots are mainly portrayed as assistants or caregivers, described as semiautonomous systems, and situated in healthcare and research contexts. Coverage relies largely on corporate and scientific sources, with a limited presence of civic or governmental voices. These representations position social robots as a key interface through which AI becomes publicly interpretable. The study contributes to research on AI and journalism in non-WEIRD contexts by showing how media representations shape understanding of emerging technologies in the absence of widespread direct experience.

articles.title: From Detection to Counterspeech: Auditing AI Moderation and Fact-Checking Practices in Ethiopia’s Multilingual Online Sphere
articles.authors: Endalkachew H. Chala
articles.abstract: AI-assisted content moderation promises to manage online incivility at scale while sparing human moderators traumatic content. Yet most evidence comes from Western languages and contexts. This study examines how AI hate-speech detection interacts with counterspeech and fact-checking in Ethiopia’s polarized Amharic and Afan Oromo spaces. Drawing on infrastructural invisibility and civic labor, it triangulates a computational audit of three classifiers against 838 hand-annotated posts (2020–2025), document analysis of platform self-descriptions and transparency reports, and 20 interviews with Ethiopian fact-checkers, volunteer flaggers, and counter-speakers. The most widely used generic classifier cannot read either language natively and, on English translations, recovers only about a tenth of hate speech; locally-oriented classifiers perform far better on Amharic but collapse on Afan Oromo, leaving it effectively unserved. Across every tool, the dominant error is under-detection, not over-removal, and the same silence recurs in platforms’ self-descriptions. Rather than sparing anyone the work, AI’s failure displaces it onto an unpaid volunteer ecology that absorbs political and psychological costs platforms benefit from yet refuse to name.

articles.title: Makeup Activism on TikTok: Beauty as Political and Visibility Work Under Platformization
articles.authors: Laura Cervi, Verena Straub
articles.abstract: Social media platforms increasingly shape how activism emerges and operates. Within these attention economies, visibility is a crucial but unevenly distributed resource, structured both by platform infrastructures and gendered power relations. This article examines how feminist actors negotiate these conditions on TikTok by mobilizing beauty practices—specifically makeup—as platform-specific resources for political expression. Focusing on two distinct cases, the Iranian #WomanLifeFreedom movement and the Latin American #NiUnaMenos protests against feminicides, the study analyzes 200 TikTok videos through comparative multimodal discourse analysis. Despite major differences in political context and risk, activists across both cases converge in their use of shared visibility strategies: They adapt TikTok’s dominant beauty formats, including makeup tutorials, transformation videos, and facial inscription, to embed feminist critique within familiar, algorithmically favored genres. By repurposing practices traditionally associated with beautification and commodification, creators transform makeup into a visual repertoire of resistance. Conceptualized here as makeup activism, these practices allow feminist content to circulate through high-visibility platform vernaculars. The article argues that visibility on TikTok is not simply a matter of exposure, but a strategic and contested resource shaped by the interaction of platform infrastructures, aesthetic conventions, and gendered politics. In doing so, it contributes to feminist media studies by moving beyond a focus on representation and providing empirical evidence on how feminist actors strategically negotiate gendered regimes of visibility across platformed public spheres that span diverse national and transnational settings.

articles.title: Mobile Media and Communication as a Post-Field? Introduction to a Special Issue on Theory
articles.authors: Lara N. Wolfers, Scott W. Campbell, Rich Ling
articles.abstract: Mobile Media and Communication (MMC) is a theoretically diverse field which lacks a single shared theoretical and methodological paradigm. Much like communication more broadly, MMC can therefore be understood as a post-field. In this Introduction to the special issue on “Mobile Communication Theory: The State of the (Post-)Field,” we describe the theoretical landscape reflected in the contributions to the special issue. The contributions span and advance a large range of research areas, bridging societal and individual approaches, software and hardware of mobile media, and different cultural perspectives. Despite this breadth, we argue that there is a shared concern across the different papers: All contributions cover the question of the distribution of power and agency across different societal actors. This shared “so what” provides a foundation for building conceptual bridges across distinct lines of inquiry. We encourage the field to cultivate additional shared points of orientation while continuing to embrace the theoretical diversity that has become one of the defining strengths of MMC.

articles.title: Greening Mobile AI?
articles.authors: Gerard Goggin
articles.abstract: Mobile AI is very much a work in progress. No better time at the outset, then, to consider its environmental implications. As mobile media and communication are woven together with AI, what are their entanglements—and what are the implications for the environment? First, given the slow progress on concerted effort over many years to tackle reuse, repair and ‘greening’ of mobile phones, as well as other mobile technology devices, and associated information and communication technologies, and the research and critique engaging with this endeavour—it is critical to consider the best focus as we move into the AI phone and beyond-the-phone future. Second, the article dissects key trends and issues—hot spots—in the environmental implications of the wider networks, infrastructures, systems and ecologies where mobiles and AI are being deployed in combination—but their ecological implications deserve greater attention. Third, the article proposes priority elements for the research and policy agenda in greening mobile AI.

articles.title: Are they virtue-signalling or sincere? The impact of perceived motives on the effectiveness of online collective action
articles.authors: Lisette Yip, Emma F. Thomas, Hawa Muhammad Farid, M. Noor Tahir
articles.abstract: Social media is an important tool used by supporters of modern social movements to persuade others to participate. However, people who engage in online collective action often face speculation about their motives and may be perceived as acting for self-serving reasons. How do these perceptions impact the effectiveness of collective action? In three experiments ( N = 916), participants viewed posts (Study 1) or an immersive social media feed (Studies 2–3) where a user encouraged them to take action for a political cause. They stated that they acted out of genuine concern (autonomous motivation), to avoid guilt and social disapproval (controlled motivation), or did not specify (baseline). Participants who viewed controlled-motivated posts perceived the user as less autonomously motivated and were therefore less likely to socially identify as supporters or take collective action. Thus, movements will be more effective at mobilising (online) support when they are seen to arise from autonomous motives.

articles.title: Cross-platformization: How U.S. right-leaning media curate their posts on Twitter and Truth Social
articles.authors: Josephine Lukito, Yini Zhang, Bin Chen, Stephen Prochaska, Meredith L. Pruden, Yunkang Yang, Wei Zhong, Megan A. Brown, Ross Dahlke, Jason Greenfield, Jiyoun Suk, Porismita Borah
articles.abstract: This study examines how seven right-leaning media organizations utilize cross-platformization strategies to reach audiences across multiple platforms; in this case, Twitter and Truth Social. Focusing on both content volume and story packaging, we collect right-leaning media organizations’ social media posts and content from the 2022 U.S. midterm election. Combining computational and qualitative methods, we find that outlets posted only a small share of total stories across the two platforms and were selective in their content, often posting only on Twitter or Truth Social. For content posted on both platforms, the outlets posted content that ideologically aligned with the users of that platform. More specifically, right-leaning outlets on Truth Social tailored their posts to ideologically aligned users.

articles.title: Two Sides of the Same Coin: Spanish Translations of the Perceived Responses to Capitalization Attempts Scale and Kessler's Perceived Social Support Scale
articles.authors: Quinn E. Hendershot, Karen Aizaga, Antonio J. Polo, Bryan Kirschen, Matthew D. Johnson
articles.abstract: Capitalization and social support within romantic dyads are linked to improved relationship functioning. Research on how these constructs impact relationship functioning is well‐established but mainly sampled on non‐Latinx White couples. To determine how these constructs function within Spanish‐speaking Latinx couples, valid Spanish‐language measures to assess them must be available. We developed Spanish translations of the Perceived Responses to Capitalization Attempts Scale and Kessler's Perceived Social Support. We utilized current best‐practice recommendations for translation and conducted a comprehensive evaluation of both measures' psychometric properties. The PRCA and KPSS both demonstrated adequate reliability, validity, and cross‐cultural and cross‐linguistic equivalence. These findings support the use of both the PRCA and the KPSS in diverse Spanish‐speaking populations. This work can help promote the inclusion of Spanish‐speakers in relationship research, thus addressing the general underrepresentation of Spanish‐speaking couples in relationship research.

articles.title: Scaling Dialogic Science Communication Training With Large Language Models
articles.authors: Elad Yacobson, Ayelet Baram-Tsabari, Ofra Amir
articles.abstract: This research note explores the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to support scalable training in science communication. Training scientists in science communication is increasingly being recognized as important, yet existing programs face scalability challenges and often prioritize one-way knowledge dissemination over dialogue. This study explores whether these challenges can be mitigated by integrating AI into the training process. We developed and empirically evaluated DiaLogic – an AI-based communication simulator. In all, 37 students engaged in two simulated dialogues and received AI-generated feedback between sessions. The results showed significant improvements in students’ performance. These findings highlight the promise of AI-based tools to support scalable science communication training.

articles.title: Constructing Online Harms: How “Trust and Safety” Translates Safety Into Risk
articles.authors: Tomás Guarna
articles.abstract: How are online harms recognized and prioritized within platform companies? Academics, journalists, and regulators have focused on identifying how digital platforms produce dangerous effects, but how harms are constructed within these organizations remains largely opaque. Based on 42 interviews with Trust and Safety specialists—the workers who define, operationalize, and create mechanisms to prevent or mitigate harmful effects—and ethnographic observation of industry forums, I describe how these workers transform concerns about platform dangers into actionable rules and processes. First, they position themselves as advocates for users, claiming moral authority to represent them within their organizations. Second, they translate abstract concerns into concrete organizational risks. Third, they publicize their companies’ harm-mitigation efforts in industry forums, performing responsiveness to critics and distributing responsibility across the sector. User harms become organizationally visible when they can be translated into corporate risks—legal liability, reputational damage, or revenue threats—and technical problems.
